title: What Consulting Teaches Us About Effective Leadership
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli and a guest co-author ask what makes leaders who grew up in consulting different, and answer with five traits: problem-solving as a reflex, pragmatic client-service resilience, selling by asking questions, treating feedback as a tool, and composure under pressure. The piece then balances the praise with three blind spots, namely defaulting to frameworks over feelings, impatience with ambiguity that cannot be controlled, and over-reliance on external validation. A short anecdote of a whiteboard framework drawn into a tense change-management meeting shows a strength becoming a liability. It closes with ten borrowable questions any leader can use when a situation is messy or unclear. The move is to treat a professional background as a toolkit whose habits must be consciously adjusted to context, which makes this a practical leadership-habits piece rather than a consulting advertisement.
points: Leaders shaped by consulting tend to persuade by asking questions that let others discover the value of an idea themselves, rather than pitching it.
Weekly or daily feedback in consulting trains leaders to detach ego from input and to seek patterns instead of praise.
The same reflexes that make consultants effective, such as structuring and solving, can flatten nuance when people need space to speak rather than a diagram.
The ten borrowed questions, such as what feedback am I avoiding because it stings, give any leader a ready prompt for foggy or urgent moments.
quotes: Leaders with a consulting background don’t pitch ideas - they guide people toward them. One of their most underrated skills? The ability to ask questions that help others see the value for themselves. Instead of leading with “here’s what we should do,” they explore impact, risk and upsides until the room agrees: “This actually makes sense.” And it works because people are more likely to back an idea they helped shape, or at least think they did.

In consulting, feedback is delivered at least weekly, and in most cases daily. It can be heavy sometimes, but mostly it’s normalised and actionable. Leaders raised in this environment learn to detach ego from input. They seek patterns, not praise, and they rarely wait for year-end reviews to course-correct.

One of the best developed traits among consulting-raised leaders? Composure. Years of navigating ambiguity, client politics and high-stakes deliverables teach them to stay focused when others start spinning. They tolerate pressure and operate effectively within it, translating complexity into clear next steps while everyone else is still digesting the problem.

Defaulting to frameworks over feelings: Not every conversation needs to be structured like a slide. In some settings, particularly with frontline staff or emotionally charged issues, your instinct to "solve" can flatten nuance.

Impatience with ambiguity you can’t control: Consultants are trained to bring clarity. However, many problems faced by leaders are messy and slow. The discomfort that used to push you toward answers might now need to be managed, not resolved.
But in that moment, structure felt like avoidance. What the team needed was space to speak, not a diagram!
